title: Parker goes to Philadelphia with Dizzy; his reading
summary: Parker went with Dizzy Gillespie to Philadelphia, then back to McShann; he read slowly and disliked reed choruses.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Was this before he was ever with McShann? Or had he been with McShann and left, and then gone back again?
Let me see. I forget... To be correct... I don't know where he was with McShann and left... I don't think so.
Because that would mean that he and Dizzy played together as early as 1938 or 1939...
Well, he come down there... When he first came there, he came and sat in with Dizzy and them, and they was working... Yeah, that's when he ended up taking him on over to Philly with him.
Yeah. He was a good get-off man. And somebody made up a little show, and Dizzy got the job, and then he went over with him.
By this stage, was Charlie able to read?
Read? Yeah, he read, but he wouldn't read fast. He didn't like to play none of them reed choruses; they was too

stiff. Everything that was augmented quarter-note, half-note, whole note, something like that, but all them sixteenth and all that syncopation stuff like that, he didn't care about foolin' with too much. He'd go along with it as long as he got somebody else playing the lead -- the lead in the section. He'd go along. He'd stay right in there with them. He didn't want you puttin' nothin' off on him by himself to lead nothin'. No. Just solos to ornament. He could do that.
Did he ever talk to you, when you and he were together a lot, about who he liked to listen to?
No, no. He always told me, 'Prof, you the king.' I said, 'Man, go ahead.' 'You the king.'
I got to get my magazines from that fellow..
Yeah. I got two that they sent me. They give me one Sunday night.
